easiness.preferred_minimum_tokens_note: Raised from 6 so the shortest sentences stop winning. A literal calque from English keeps English's short function-word skeleton, which is exactly the shape frequency-burden rewards: on French, 'Nous y allons mais vous non.' ranked FIRST for four separate cards. This does not fix the ranking, it stops the most skeletal sentences taking the head of the queue.

pooling.note: How wide a card samples before quality cuts it to budget, and what counts against a sentence's form. Every weight here judges how well made a sentence is; none of them can prefer one sense of the target word over another, which is what lets quality be applied as hard as the supply allows. The multiplier is a starting value, not a measured one: comparing sense distributions at 2x, 3x and 5x after a WSD run is what would settle it.

quality.apply_form_rules_to_translation_note: The form rules above were written for the target and applied only there. The English side is what a learner reads for meaning, so a fragment there is exactly as useless: "What was he doing", "I bought the agreement back from them for two million..." cut mid-clause. Measured on the shipped 1,000-card decks: 0.4% of Portuguese displayed examples, 0.4% of Spanish, 1.2% of Czech.
quality.fragment_note: A subtitle row is a slice of a stream: it can begin partway through one sentence and end partway through the next. A row starting lowercase is a continuation of the row before it, and one ending in a comma, semicolon or colon stops before its clause closes. Both read as broken language rather than as an example. Measured on the shipped decks: 3.4% and 0.7% of Czech displayed examples, 0.4% and 0.3% of Portuguese.
quality.minimum_distinct_ratio_note: How much of the sentence is new rather than echoed. Probed against real harvested Portuguese: every degenerate line scored 0.67 or below ('O que? O que e que eu...' 0.57) and every natural one 0.83 or above, so the boundary sits in an empty gap. Drops 1,718 of 120,000 candidates.
quality.minimum_distinct_tokens_note: Lowered from 6. Six was a patch for a bug since fixed at source: easiness measured burden over distinct words but length over raw tokens, so repetition padded a sentence past the short-sentence penalty and scored a perfect 0.0. With length now measured on the same basis, and minimum_distinct_ratio catching echoes, six was a subtitle-era compensation discarding a quarter of the better corpus -- it rejected 28% of Spanish Tatoeba records, whose sentences are legitimately short at a 5.1-word mean.
quality.reject_subtitle_annotations_note: Speaker labels ("HENRY:"), sound cues ("[Groans]", "(phone rings)") and the dash separating two speakers inside one subtitle row are production notes, not language. Applied to both sides. Measured on the shipped decks: 0.5% of Portuguese displayed examples, 0.3% of Spanish, 0.7% of Czech. Two Spanish examples had a sound cue as the entire English side.
quality.reject_truncated_fragments_note: A line cut mid-thought is grammatical and teaches nothing: the clause the target belongs to was never finished. Measured on the Portuguese pilot: 6.5% of candidates, and no card fell below the five it must display (lowest pool 48 of 60).

scan.note: Read every corpus whole. This used to stop once 95% of cards had filled their budget, which was the right trade when a 9,999-card Spanish scan cost 2,001 seconds: 95% of cards were satisfied by 19% of the corpus. The pooled sampler and the matcher rewrite took that scan to 64 seconds, and the stop was demonstrably throwing away real vocabulary -- it read 1,366,962 of Spanish's 4,236,176 subtitle rows, and `arzobispo` (71 occurrences, an ordinary word) harvested nothing because every one of them lay past the cut. Reading the whole corpus costs 130 seconds instead of 64 and takes cards holding fifteen or more candidates from 95.1% to 98.8%, cards under fifteen from 485 to 120, and cards with nothing at all from 19 to 7 -- the 7 being OCR artifacts and film proper nouns that genuinely do not occur. The ceiling stays as a guard against a corpus larger than any we hold (Czech 2015-plus, the biggest, is 7.55M rows).
